name: Nasal breathing meta

lead: The nasal breathing meta is the habit of breathing through the nose instead of the mouth, with the goal of a stronger jaw and midface, a better profile and a less bloated face. It is closely tied to mewing, mouth taping and discussions of nasal surgery.

Proponents say breathing pattern and tongue posture influence the growing jaw and midface. Research links chronic mouth breathing in children to facial growth patterns, sometimes called long face syndrome, and a systematic review and meta-analysis examined its effect on facial skeletal development, though cause can run in either direction. Studies on adults who switch to nasal breathing are much thinner.

paras: Users make nose breathing a default during the day and exercise, add mouth tape at night, and pair it with mewing posture. People with blocked noses often look at the obstruction first, since nasal obstruction is a main cause of mouth breathing.

Breathing through the nose is normal physiology. Mouth taping is little researched and is described as risky for anyone with nasal blockage or sleep apnea. Nasal surgery such as turbinate reduction carries surgical risks, and some users raise empty nose syndrome.

chain: Claimed better jaw and midface development
angle.text: Users favour nasal breathing, sometimes with mouth taping, for a stronger jaw and midface and a leaner-looking face. Studies in children link mouth breathing to growth changes; whether switching as an adult changes appearance has not been tested.

lead: The nasal breathing meta is the looksmaxxing belief that habitually breathing through the nose, with the lips closed and the tongue resting against the palate, supports the growth and shape of the jaws and midface, and therefore how the face looks. Proponents connect it to a forward-set jaw, a well-defined profile, an open airway and better sleep, and it is usually discussed alongside mewing, mouth taping, myofunctional exercises, palatal expansion and nasal surgery [1][2].

The idea draws on a genuine body of orthodontic and ENT literature. Chronic mouth breathing in children has been associated with a longer lower face, backward-rotated jaws, a steeper occlusal plane and a narrower airway, a pattern often called long face syndrome, although clinicians note the relationship may run in both directions [3][4][5]. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled ten studies on the subject [4]. Research on adults is much more limited, and the looksmaxxing claim that switching to nasal breathing after growth has finished reshapes the face has not been tested in published studies.

In practice the meta covers a spectrum: keeping the lips sealed by day, clearing a blocked nose with sprays or allergy treatment, taping the mouth shut at night, wearing nasal strips, practising tongue posture, and in some cases seeking ENT procedures or expansion treatments for nasal obstruction [6]. Popular books such as James Nestor's Breath and the Buteyko tradition of breathing retraining gave the idea a wider audience beyond appearance forums [7][8].

paras: Nasal breathing filters, warms and humidifies incoming air, and the nose is described as the body's normal route for breathing at rest [9][10]. Chronic mouth breathing is reported to arise in most cases as an adaptation to nasal congestion, which may appear only during sleep, and less often from lip incompetence or anatomical causes [3]. The meta takes this medical observation and extends it into a looks framework: if a child who breathes through the mouth tends to develop a longer, narrower face, then keeping the mouth closed and the nose open should favour the opposite pattern.

In forum usage the term covers three things. The first is a daytime habit of lips-together nasal breathing, usually paired with a tongue-posture practice. The second is clearing obstruction, through nasal sprays, allergy management, sleep-apnea screening, or procedures such as septoplasty, turbinate reduction and functional rhinoplasty. The third is night-time measures such as mouth taping, chin straps or nasal strips [6][11].

Concern with mouth breathing predates the internet by well over a century. The American painter and author George Catlin, who travelled to the American West several times in the 1830s, published a book in 1862 titled The Breath of Life, later retitled Shut Your Mouth and Save Your Life. He observed what he took to be a preference for nose breathing among Native American communities and noted that mothers closed their infants' mouths during sleep [3].

In the early twentieth century physicians used the term mouth-breather clinically for children breathing orally because of obstruction; a 1903 school hygiene book, The Hygiene of the Schoolroom, used it in a photo caption [3]. Yoga teacher B. K. S. Iyengar later summarised the nose-for-breathing principle in the phrase that the nose is for breathing and the mouth is for eating [3].

In the 1950s the Ukrainian physiologist Konstantin Buteyko developed a breathing-retraining method in the Soviet Union that emphasised nasal breathing, including at night. It later spread to Australia, New Zealand, Britain and the United States, mainly as an asthma approach [8]. In orthodontics, the British orthodontist John Mew (1928-2025) proposed in 1958 what he called the Tropic Premise, that oral posture and function strongly influence jaw growth, and developed orthotropics after a 1968 visit to Rolf Fränkel in East Germany. It combined palatal expansion with a recommended tongue resting position [12]. His son Mike Mew carried the ideas onto social media, where interest in mewing rose from about January 2019 according to Google Trends [2].

James Nestor's Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art (Riverhead, May 2020) argued that modern humans have drifted toward chronic mouth breathing and that returning to nasal breathing can improve health. It spent 18 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list in its first year, has sold over a million copies and was a finalist for the 2021 Royal Society Science Book Prize [7]. Mouth taping gained wider attention around the same period; one account of Buteyko-related practice notes that a 2019 post by Indonesian singer Andien showing tape over her family's mouths drew interest to the method [8].

The orthodontic version of the theory holds that the tongue resting on the palate acts as a natural expander of the upper jaw, whereas an open mouth lets the tongue drop and the face grow downward. Reviews of mouth breathing describe a related chain: nasal obstruction leads to open-mouth posture, chronic tension in the muscles around the mouth, a backward mandibular position and a narrow maxillary arch, with class II malocclusion, crossbite and open bite as common dental findings [5]. A review of dysventilation by French authors describes it as a functional disorder able to disrupt facial morphogenesis and proposes orthodontic care with orofacial myofunctional therapy for children, and better oro-cranio-facial balance for adults; the authors note the published data are of uneven methodological quality [13].

Another strand concerns inflammation and airway tissue. One proposed sequence runs from inflammation to adenoid and tissue growth, airway obstruction and then altered facial structure, which would make treating the obstruction the first step [3]. Wikipedia's mouth breathing entry also reports that nasal breathing produces nitric oxide and that mouth breathing is linked with gum inflammation, dental plaque and anterior open bite [3].

Looksmaxxing communities add the idea of a feedback loop: a recessed jaw narrows the airway, narrowing encourages mouth breathing, and that in turn reinforces the recession. Proponents describe nasal breathing as the habit that breaks the loop [1][6].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Oral Health (Zhao and colleagues) searched six databases through February 2020 and included ten studies of children with mouth-breathing-related changes. Mouth-breathing children had lower SNA and SNB values, indicating a more backward position of the upper and lower jaw, higher vertical measures, a steeper occlusal plane, labially inclined upper incisors and narrower airway dimensions. The authors concluded that the jaws tended to rotate backward and downward [4].

A 2010 Laryngoscope study compared mouth breathing and nasal breathing in orthodontic patients' dentofacial and craniofacial development. A 2015 Polish review summarised the oral and craniofacial manifestations of mouth breathing in children, including posterior mandibular position, narrow maxillary arch, class II malocclusion and crossbite [5]. Rapid palatal expansion has been reviewed for its effect on nose breathing and sleep apnea in children; the review concluded it is predominantly recommended for children with maxillary constriction and that collaboration between pediatricians, ENT doctors and orthodontists gives the best outcomes [14]. A 2025 randomized trial measured skeletal and nasal airflow changes in late adolescents and young adults after conventional versus miniscrew-assisted expansion.

Mouth taping has been studied mostly in sleep-medicine populations. A 2009 randomized, single-blind crossover trial of 51 adults with asthma used microporous tape at night as in the Buteyko method; participants found it acceptable, but the abstract reports no differences in the main asthma outcomes [15]. A 2022 preliminary study of 20 mouth-breathers with mild obstructive sleep apnea found median apnea-hypopnea index fell from 8.3 to 4.7 events per hour with silicone tape, with 13 participants classed as responders; the authors called for larger trials [16]. A 2024 nonrandomized trial in JAMA Otolaryngology of 54 analysed patients found that manual mouth closure during sedated endoscopy increased inspiratory airflow on average, but airflow fell in people who breathed mainly through the mouth and had velopharyngeal obstruction [17]. A 2025 PLoS One systematic review of ten studies covering 213 patients found two with significant improvement in sleep-apnea markers and judged that taping without screening carried potentially serious risk, particularly where the nose is obstructed [18].

None of these studies measures facial appearance after taping or after adult nasal-breathing training. Nasal strips were tested in 1990s trials: a polysomnographic study examined their effect on snoring, a German randomized trial reported no effect on sleep apnea and snoring [19], and a small treadmill study found no differences in maximal oxygen consumption with a nasal dilator [20]. Wikipedia reports that strips increase volume in the front of the nasal cavity and that wearers often report breathing more easily [11].

Functional rhinoplasty and septal or turbinate surgery are described in reviews as treatments for nasal obstruction. Maxillary expansion, including miniscrew-assisted versions, is discussed in some communities as a way of enlarging the nasal airway, and trials have measured airflow changes afterwards [14]. Nasal strips are sold over the counter, with skin irritation the main reported side effect [11]. Orofacial myofunctional therapy, a program of tongue and lip exercises, is proposed in the orthodontic literature as part of managing mouth breathing [13].

On looksmax.org, nasal breathing threads move between sincere troubleshooting and mockery of mewing culture. One user in his twenties with a recessed jaw and a mildly blocked nose asked about sprays, taping, jaw straps and apnea screening; one reply used the thread to ridicule Mike Mew and said taping would simply disrupt sleep, while another said nasal sprays helped but should not be used every day [6]. Another thread asked whether taping damages the skin or stretches the lips; replies said skin regenerates and that the poster did it nearly nightly [21]. A further thread compares maxillary skeletal expansion with turbinate reduction or septoplasty, with one user citing empty nose syndrome as a risk and another calling expansion procedures gimmicks.

Mewing as a whole is widely covered in mainstream media. Wikipedia reports that interest spread rapidly on social media, especially in looksmaxxing and incel subcultures, that the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence it improves the jaw, and that Mike Mew was struck from the UK dental register in 2024 [2]. Grokipedia describes nasal breathing as a recommended habit among mewing proponents and mouth taping as risky without professional supervision [1].

Tape over the mouth can be a hazard when the nose is blocked, which is why the 2025 review recommends screening before use [18]. Surgery for obstruction carries ordinary operative risks. Empty nose syndrome, a sensation of suffocation despite a clear airway usually following turbinate surgery, is debated: some ENT specialists accept it as a distinct condition while others attribute symptoms to psychological causes, and French guidelines advise keeping at least two thirds of the inferior turbinate [22]. Palatal expansion in people with normal occlusion has been described in a review as a last-resort option for airway problems [14].

Orthotropics itself remains disputed. Wikipedia reports that the theory contains some plausible conclusions but that evidence for the treatment is inadequate, and records a series of regulatory actions against John and Mike Mew by the UK General Dental Council [12][2]. Buteyko-style breathing retraining is described as lacking clear evidence of effectiveness in a 2015 Australian government review, while a 2014 British asthma guideline said it may improve some symptoms [8].

lore.intro: Nasal breathing is treated in these communities as a foundation habit for facial development and airway, linked to mewing and sometimes to surgical options, with frequent disagreement between sincere practitioners and sceptics [6][1].
